summary: Specifies the algorithms, parameters, key formats, key sizes and signature format for RPKI subscribers who sign certificates, revocation lists and signed objects, and for relying parties who check them. It was replaced by RFC 7935.

plainLanguage.summary: To keep locks compatible, everyone must use the same kind of key and signature. This lists which ones RPKI uses. It was later replaced by RFC 7935.

questions: which signature algorithm does rpki use
subtitle: Cryptographic algorithms and key sizes for RPKI

tldr.problem: RPKI implementations need a standardized cryptographic profile to ensure all operators use compatible algorithms and key sizes for signing certificates, revocation lists, and routing objects.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6485 specifies that RPKI uses RSA with PKCS #1 v1.5 signatures combined with SHA-256 hashing, 2048-bit RSA keys with public exponent 65537, and defines how these algorithms are represented in certificates, CRLs, and CMS SignedData.
tldr.outcome: RPKI deployments achieved interoperability by standardizing on a single, well-understood cryptographic approach. RFC 7935 later replaced this profile with support for additional algorithms.

today: RFC 6485 remains a Proposed Standard and is still referenced by RPKI specifications. However, RFC 7935 extended the RPKI algorithm profile to support additional algorithms and provides a path for future evolution beyond RSA-based cryptography.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6485 specifies the cryptographic algorithms, key formats, key sizes, and signature formats used throughout the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI). RPKI is the public key infrastructure for validating the authenticity and authorization of Internet routing information, particularly for BGP route origin authorizations and IP address allocations.

This specification applies to all RPKI subscribers who generate digital signatures on certificates, Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs), and signed objects such as Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) and manifests. It also applies to relying parties who must verify these signatures. The document is referenced by other RPKI specifications including the RPKI Certificate Policy (RFC 6484), the RPKI Certificate Profile (RFC 6487), and the SIDR Architecture (RFC 6480).
sections.plainLanguage: RPKI is the system that checks if a company really owns an IP address or can tell routers where traffic should go. Everyone doing this checking needs to use the same lock design so it works everywhere.

sections.title: Signature and Hash Algorithms
sections.content:
RPKI uses a single mandatory cryptographic approach: RSA PKCS #1 v1.5 signatures combined with SHA-256 hashing. When referenced together, this combination is termed "RSA with SHA-256." The Object Identifier (OID) sha256withRSAEncryption from RFC 4055 must be used in all RPKI cryptographic operations.

The SHA-256 hash algorithm appears in different locations depending on the context. In certificates and CRLs, SHA-256 is implicitly combined with the signature algorithm. In Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) SignedData structures, SHA-256 is identified separately using the OID and parameters defined in RFC 5754. One exception to SHA-256 usage is the generation of authority and subject key identifiers in certificates, which uses SHA-1 for historical compatibility as specified in RFC 6487.

The OID sha256withRSAEncryption appears in specific fields of different structures: the signature and signatureAlgorithm fields of certificates, the signatureAlgorithm field of CRLs, the signatureAlgorithm field of CMS SignerInfo, and the signature field of PKCS #10 certification requests or CRMF Certificate Request Message Format requests.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone locks things with RSA keys and checks for tampering with SHA-256. This combination is called RSA with SHA-256. It appears in different parts of different documents depending on what they are.

sections.title: Asymmetric Keys and Key Pair Formats
sections.content:
All RPKI cryptographic operations use RSA key pairs with precisely specified parameters. The RSA modulus must be exactly 2048 bits long, and the public exponent must be 65537 (a value commonly written as 0x10001 in hexadecimal). These parameters are chosen for security and compatibility: 2048-bit keys provide adequate security for signing infrastructure, and the public exponent 65537 is a widely supported standard value.

The public key is encoded in the subjectPublicKeyInfo structure as defined in RFC 5280. This structure contains an algorithm field identifying the key type and an RSAPublicKey field containing the actual public key material. For the algorithm field, the object identifier for RSA PKCS #1 v1.5 with SHA-256 and its associated parameters (as specified in RFC 4055) must be used.

The format of private keys is determined by local policy and is not specified by RFC 6485. Different RPKI implementations may use different private key storage formats, as long as the corresponding public key and signatures conform to the requirements above.
sections.plainLanguage: RSA keys must be 2048 bits long and use the standard public exponent 65537. How you store your private key is up to you, but the public part must follow these exact rules.

sections.title: Signature Encoding Formats
sections.content:
The structure for encoding signatures varies slightly depending on the context. In certificates, signatures are encoded as specified in Section 1.2 of RFC 4055. In CMS SignedData structures, signatures are encoded as specified in RFC 3370, which defines how PKCS #1 v1.5 signatures appear within the broader CMS framework.

These encoding specifications ensure that all RPKI implementations produce and consume signatures in a compatible format. By using standard, well-defined encoding rules, RPKI achieves interoperability: a signature generated by one implementation can be verified by any other implementation following these standards.
sections.plainLanguage: Signatures are written in a standard format that everyone understands. There are slightly different formats for different document types, but they all mean the same thing.

sections.title: Future Algorithm Evolution
sections.content:
RFC 6485 explicitly anticipates that RPKI will eventually need to adopt stronger cryptographic algorithms and larger key sizes as computational power increases and security standards evolve. The specification notes that this profile should be replaced with updated requirements when necessary to maintain adequate cryptographic security for protecting the integrity of RPKI signed products.

To facilitate a smooth transition to stronger algorithms in the future, both CAs and relying parties should design their systems to support multiple RPKI algorithm profiles simultaneously. This capability allows for a phased, orderly transition where older algorithms are gradually deprecated while new algorithms are introduced. Organizations implementing RPKI systems should plan for the eventual need to migrate away from 2048-bit RSA and SHA-256 to stronger alternatives when this RFC is updated.
sections.plainLanguage: As computers get faster, locks need to get stronger. In the future, RPKI will probably switch to bigger keys and harder locks. Right now, systems should be ready to use more than one kind of lock at the same time, to make switching easier later.
